reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / IDSA
clinicalPearls: Infection typically complicates a neuropathic or neuroischaemic ulcer and is diagnosed clinically by local signs of inflammation or purulence, not by culture alone
Peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease, and poor glycaemic control combine to create and perpetuate the wound
Severity should be graded (mild, moderate, severe) to guide the need for hospitalisation, imaging, and route of therapy
Mild infections are often caused by staphylococci and streptococci, while chronic, previously treated, or severe wounds tend to be polymicrobial with Gram-negatives and anaerobes
Probing to bone or an ulcer that is large, deep, or long-standing raises the likelihood of underlying osteomyelitis
Assessment of the arterial supply is essential, as ischaemia impairs healing and antibiotic delivery and may require revascularisation
Management principles combine wound debridement, pressure offloading, glycaemic control, vascular assessment, and antibiotics targeted to severity and likely organisms
Deep abscess, extensive necrosis, or gas-forming infection requires urgent surgical drainage or debridement
reference.pathophysiology: Diabetic foot infection develops when skin integrity is breached, usually over a pressure point, in a foot compromised by sensory neuropathy (loss of protective sensation), motor and autonomic dysfunction (deformity and dry, fissured skin), and often peripheral arterial disease. Impaired neutrophil function and microvascular disease blunt the immune response and reduce tissue perfusion, allowing colonising skin flora to invade soft tissue, tendon sheaths, and bone. Infection can spread rapidly along fascial and tendon planes, producing deep abscesses and osteomyelitis.
additionalDifferentials: Uninfected neuropathic ulcer with colonisation only
Gout or acute crystal arthropathy of the foot
Deep vein thrombosis causing a swollen limb
infectionMimics: Charcot foot presenting as a warm, swollen, erythematous foot
Cellulitis mimicked by lipodermatosclerosis or venous stasis changes
Acute gouty arthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint
Contact dermatitis around a chronic wound dressing
additionalInvestigations: Deep tissue or bone specimens for culture rather than superficial swabs
Inflammatory markers and glucose or HbA1c to gauge control
Plain radiographs, with MRI when osteomyelitis or deep collection is suspected
Vascular assessment including ankle-brachial index and arterial imaging
redFlags: Deep abscess, extensive necrosis, or gas in tissues requiring urgent surgical drainage or debridement
Rapidly spreading infection with systemic toxicity indicating limb- or life-threatening sepsis
Critical limb ischaemia threatening tissue viability and demanding urgent vascular input
Probing to bone or radiographic bone destruction suggesting osteomyelitis
reference.prognosis: Outcomes depend on infection severity, adequacy of perfusion, and glycaemic control; mild soft-tissue infection often resolves, whereas deep infection with ischaemia or osteomyelitis carries a substantial risk of amputation and is associated with reduced long-term survival.
pitfalls: Treating on the basis of a superficial swab that reflects colonisation rather than a deep specimen
Overlooking peripheral arterial disease that undermines healing and antibiotic delivery
Missing underlying osteomyelitis and treating for too short a duration
Neglecting offloading and debridement while relying on antibiotics alone
management: Start empirical antibiotics guided by severity, covering staphylococci and streptococci in mild infection and broadening to Gram-negative and anaerobic cover in severe, chronic or previously treated polymicrobial wounds, then de-escalate to deep tissue or bone culture
Undertake urgent surgical debridement of necrotic and infected tissue, drainage of any abscess, and resection of infected bone where osteomyelitis is confirmed
Offload pressure from the wound, provide meticulous wound care and dressings, and optimise glycaemic control to support healing
Assess arterial perfusion and refer for revascularisation of the ischaemic limb, since ischaemia impairs healing and antibiotic delivery
Grade infection severity to direct hospitalisation and route of therapy, and use inflammatory markers and MRI to detect deep collections or osteomyelitis
Manage through a specialist multidisciplinary diabetic foot team spanning podiatry, vascular surgery, infectious diseases and diabetology
Escalate to inpatient intravenous therapy for severe or systemically unwell patients, and consider amputation when infection is limb-threatening or uncontrolled
